quick.summary: Your average went up and revenue went down. Both can be true.
quick.takeaway: Never read an average without the count beside it.

parts.title: The average that went up
parts.cliff: Three questions catch it every time.

beats.line: Average order value is up a third. So why is revenue down?
Both are true. Want to see how?
Please. And no formulas.
Picture a tea stall. Ten customers in week one.
Eight buy a tea. Two buy a big lunch.
Four hundred rupees. Forty rupees a head.
Fine. Forty. What changes?
Week two. Four tea drinkers stop coming.
The lunch crowd still shows up. Same two people.
Now the stall takes three hundred and twenty.
Wait. Less money, but the average went up?
Up by a third. And nobody spent a rupee more.
Then how do I ever trust an average?

parts.title: Three questions before you trust it

beats.line: So averages lie. Do I stop using them?
No. You ask three questions first.
One. How many are in it?
Ten became six. The crowd shrank.
Two. Who left?
Three. Split it by group.
Each group spent exactly what it spent before.
Analysts call this a mix shift.
Can I just say the crowd changed?
You can. That is exactly what it means.
So when someone cheers an average, I ask for the count.
The count first. Then who left.

quiz.question: If the average order value rises, customers must be spending more.
quiz.explanation: The average also rises when low spenders leave. Nobody has to spend more.

quiz.question: Average basket size jumped this month. What do you check first?
options: How many orders are in the average
Which day had the highest sales
quiz.explanation: The count tells you whether the crowd changed. If it shrank, find out who left before reading the average.
